title: Solutions
subject: Chemistry

blocks.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more chemically non-reacting substances whose composition can vary within certain limits.

items: Solvent: The component present in a larger amount, which generally determines the physical state of the solution.
Solute: The component that dissolves in the solvent and is generally present in a smaller amount.

blocks.text: Example: In a sugar solution, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
Solutions are classified into three types based on the physical states of the solute and solvent.
A solid solute dissolves in a liquid solvent. Example: Sugar in water.
A gas dissolves in a liquid solvent. Example: Carbon dioxide in soda water.
One solid is uniformly mixed with another solid. Example: Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc.
The solute and solvent can each exist as a solid, liquid or gas. Therefore, nine types of solutions are possible.

blocks.label: Classification of solutions based on physical states

blocks.text: *These are illustrative classifications; the actual formation of a homogeneous solution depends on the substances and conditions.
Important: Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases, and brass is a solid solution.
The concentration of a solution is the amount of solute present in a given amount of solvent or solution. Concentration is expressed in the following ways.
It is the mass of solute present in 100 g of solution.
Example: 10 g of sugar is dissolved in 90 g of water.
It is the volume of solute present in 100 mL of solution.
Example: A solution containing 20 mL of ethanol in 100 mL of solution has a volume percentage of 20%.
It is the mass of solute present in 100 mL of solution.
\[\text{Mass by volume \%} = \frac{\text{Mass of solute (g)}}{\text{Volume of solution (mL)}} \times 100\]
Example: A solution containing 5 g of glucose in 100 mL of solution has a mass by volume percentage of 5%.
It is used to express the concentration of very dilute solutions.

The numerator and denominator must be expressed in the same units.

For dilute aqueous solutions, \(1\text{ ppm} \approx 1\text{ mg/L}\).

blocks.text: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution. A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve under the given conditions. Solubility mainly depends on:

items: Nature of the solute and solvent.
Temperature.
Pressure, especially for gases dissolved in liquids.

notes.heading: 1.3.1 Solubility of a Solid in a Liquid

blocks.text: The solubility of a solid in a liquid depends mainly on the nature of the solute, the nature of the solvent and temperature.
1. Effect of Nature of Solute and Solvent
The solubility of a substance depends on the intermolecular forces between solute and solvent particles. Generally, like dissolves like.

items: Polar substances tend to dissolve in polar solvents.
Non-polar substances tend to dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Sodium chloride dissolves in water because of favourable ion–dipole interactions.
Iodine dissolves more readily in non-polar solvents such as carbon tetrachloride than in water.

blocks.text: The effect of temperature on solubility depends on whether the dissolution process absorbs or releases heat. Endothermic dissolution: Heat is absorbed during dissolution. Solubility generally increases with an increase in temperature.
Exothermic dissolution: Heat is released during dissolution. Solubility generally decreases with an increase in temperature.
For many solid solutes, solubility increases with temperature, but this is not true for every substance.
Pressure has very little effect on the solubility of solids in liquids because solids and liquids are nearly incompressible.

notes.heading: 1.3.2 Solubility of a Gas in a Liquid (Henry's Law)

blocks.text: The solubility of a gas in a liquid depends mainly on the nature of the gas and solvent, temperature, and pressure.
Henry's law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid. Mathematically,

items: \(p\) = partial pressure of the gas above the solution.
\(x\) = mole fraction of the gas dissolved in the solution.
\(K_H\) = Henry's law constant.

blocks.text: Thus, increasing the partial pressure of a gas increases its solubility in the liquid at constant temperature.

items: Carbonated drinks: Carbon dioxide is dissolved in soft drinks under high pressure. When the bottle is opened, the pressure decreases and carbon dioxide escapes as bubbles.

Scuba diving: At high pressures underwater, more nitrogen dissolves in the blood. If a diver ascends too quickly, the pressure decreases and dissolved nitrogen may form bubbles, causing decompression sickness.
High altitudes: At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower. Consequently, less oxygen dissolves in the blood, which can cause difficulty in breathing.
Gas solubility increases with increasing pressure at constant temperature.
For most gases, solubility decreases as temperature increases.
A higher value of \(K_H\) indicates lower gas solubility at a given pressure, according to \(x = p / K_H\).

blocks.text: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid when the vapour is in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container at a given temperature. When a liquid is kept in a closed container, some of its molecules escape from the surface into the vapour phase. At the same time, some vapour molecules return to the liquid. When the rates of evaporation and condensation become equal, dynamic equilibrium is established. The pressure exerted by the vapour at this stage is called the equilibrium vapour pressure.

notes.heading: 1.4.2 Raoult’s Law as a Special Case of Henry’s Law

blocks.text: Henry’s law states that the partial pressure of a gas above a solution is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.
Raoult’s law states that the partial vapour pressure of a volatile component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.
Comparing the two equations, we find that Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law when the Henry’s law constant is equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component.

Thus, Raoult’s law can be considered a special case of Henry’s law in which the proportionality constant becomes equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component.

For an ideal solution, the component obeys Raoult’s law over the entire range of composition.

notes.heading: 1.4.3 Vapour Pressure of Solutions of Solids in Liquids

blocks.text:
When a non-volatile solid solute is dissolved in a volatile liquid solvent, only the solvent contributes significantly to the vapour pressure of the solution.

For example, when sugar is dissolved in water, sugar does not evaporate appreciably. Therefore, the vapour pressure of the solution is due to water alone.

According to Raoult’s law,

items: \(p_1\) = vapour pressure of the solution.
\(x_1\) = mole fraction of the solvent.
\(p_1^\circ\) = vapour pressure of the pure solvent.

blocks.text: Since the solute is non-volatile, its presence decreases the mole fraction of the solvent. Hence, the vapour pressure of the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent.
The lowering of vapour pressure is the difference between the vapour pressure of the pure solvent and that of the solution.
Therefore, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is

Thus, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the non-volatile solute for an ideal dilute solution.

This is a colligative property because it depends on the number of solute particles present relative to the number of solvent particles, rather than on the chemical nature of the solute.
An ideal solution is a solution that obeys Raoult’s law over the entire range of composition at a given temperature. For a binary solution containing volatile components A and B,

items: They obey Raoult’s law at all compositions.
The intermolecular forces between A–B molecules are nearly equal to those between A–A and B–B molecules.
The enthalpy change on mixing is zero: \(\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0\).
The volume change on mixing is zero: \(\Delta V_{\text{mix}} = 0\).
Benzene and toluene.
n-Hexane and n-heptane.

blocks.text: A non-ideal solution is a solution that does not obey Raoult’s law over the entire range of composition. Non-ideal behaviour occurs when the intermolecular forces between unlike molecules (A–B) differ significantly from those between like molecules (A–A and B–B). Non-ideal solutions show two types of deviations.

A solution shows positive deviation when its observed vapour pressure is greater than the vapour pressure predicted by Raoult’s law. This occurs when A–B intermolecular attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B attractions. The molecules escape more easily into the vapour phase. Characteristics:

items: Vapour pressure is higher than the ideal value.
Enthalpy change on mixing is generally positive: \(\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0\).
Volume change on mixing is generally positive: \(\Delta V_{\text{mix}} > 0\).

blocks.text: Examples: Ethanol and acetone; ethanol and cyclohexane.

A solution shows negative deviation when its observed vapour pressure is lower than the vapour pressure predicted by Raoult’s law. This occurs when A–B intermolecular attractions are stronger than A–A and B–B attractions. The molecules escape less easily into the vapour phase. Characteristics:

items: Vapour pressure is lower than the ideal value.
Enthalpy change on mixing is generally negative: \(\Delta H_{\text{mix}} < 0\).
Volume change on mixing is generally negative: \(\Delta V_{\text{mix}} < 0\).

blocks.text: Examples: Acetone and chloroform; nitric acid and water.

Azeotropes are liquid mixtures that boil at a constant temperature and have the same composition in the liquid and vapour phases. Therefore, they cannot be completely separated into their components by simple fractional distillation. Azeotropes are of two types.
These are formed by solutions showing sufficiently large positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

items: They have a lower boiling point than either pure component.
Their vapour pressure is higher than expected for an ideal solution.

blocks.text: These are formed by solutions showing sufficiently large negative deviation from Raoult’s law.

items: They have a higher boiling point than either pure component.
Their vapour pressure is lower than expected for an ideal solution.

notes.heading: 1.6 Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

blocks.text: Colligative properties are the properties of dilute solutions that depend on the number of solute particles present relative to the number of solvent particles, and not on the chemical nature of the solute. These properties are mainly observed when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a volatile solvent. There are four main colligative properties:

items: Relative lowering of vapour pressure.
Elevation of boiling point.
Depression of freezing point.
Osmotic pressure.

The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external pressure. When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, the vapour pressure of the solvent decreases. Therefore, the solution must be heated to a higher temperature to make its vapour pressure equal to the external pressure. Hence, the boiling point of the solution is higher than that of the pure solvent. This increase is called elevation of boiling point.
It is the difference between the boiling point of the solution and that of the pure solvent.

items: \(T_b\) = boiling point of the solution.
\(T_b^\circ\) = boiling point of the pure solvent.

blocks.text: For dilute solutions, the elevation of boiling point is directly proportional to the molality of the solution.

items: \(K_b\) = molal elevation constant or ebullioscopic constant.
\(m\) = molality of the solution.

blocks.text: The value of \(K_b\) depends on the nature of the solvent.

\(w_2\) = mass of solute in grams.
\(M_2\) = molar mass of solute in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(K_b\) = ebullioscopic constant.

blocks.text: Unit of \(K_b\): \(\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). Elevation of boiling point is a colligative property because, for dilute solutions, it depends on the number of dissolved solute particles rather than their chemical identity.

The freezing point of a liquid is the temperature at which its liquid and solid phases coexist in equilibrium. When a non-volatile solute is dissolved in a solvent, the freezing point of the solution becomes lower than that of the pure solvent. This decrease is called depression of freezing point. For example, adding salt to ice lowers its freezing point, which helps in melting ice at temperatures below \(0^\circ\text{C}\).
It is the difference between the freezing point of the pure solvent and that of the solution.

items: \(T_f^\circ\) = freezing point of the pure solvent.
\(T_f\) = freezing point of the solution.

blocks.text: For dilute solutions, depression of freezing point is directly proportional to the molality of the solution.

items: \(K_f\) = molal depression constant or cryoscopic constant.
\(m\) = molality of the solution.

blocks.text: The value of \(K_f\) depends on the nature of the solvent.

items: \(w_1\) = mass of solvent in grams.
\(w_2\) = mass of solute in grams.
\(M_2\) = molar mass of solute in \(\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(K_f\) = cryoscopic constant.

blocks.text: Unit of \(K_f\): \(\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\). Depression of freezing point is a colligative property because, for dilute solutions, it depends on the number of dissolved solute particles rather than their chemical identity.

Osmosis is the spontaneous movement of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration. A semipermeable membrane allows solvent molecules to pass through it but prevents the passage of solute particles. Example: When raisins are placed in water, water enters the raisins through their membranes, causing them to swell.
Osmotic pressure is the minimum external pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop osmosis. It is represented by the symbol \(\pi\). For dilute solutions, osmotic pressure is given by

blocks.text: The molar mass of a solute calculated using colligative properties may sometimes differ from its actual molar mass. This is called abnormal molar mass. Abnormal molar mass occurs when solute particles undergo association or dissociation in a solution, changing the total number of particles present.

Association occurs when two or more solute molecules combine to form a larger particle. Due to association, the total number of solute particles decreases. Consequently, the observed colligative property becomes smaller than expected, and the experimentally calculated molar mass becomes higher than the actual molar mass. Example: Ethanoic acid molecules associate to form dimers in benzene through hydrogen bonding.

Dissociation occurs when a solute separates into two or more particles in a solution. Due to dissociation, the total number of solute particles increases. Consequently, the observed colligative property becomes greater than expected, and the experimentally calculated molar mass becomes lower than the actual molar mass. Example: Sodium chloride dissociates into sodium and chloride ions in water.
The van ’t Hoff factor is the ratio of the observed colligative property to the calculated colligative property when the solute is assumed to remain undissociated.
It can also be expressed as the ratio of the normal molar mass to the experimentally determined molar mass.
Values of the Van ’t Hoff Factor

items: For non-electrolytes that neither associate nor dissociate: \(i = 1\)
For association: \(i < 1\)
For dissociation: \(i > 1\)

summary: Chapter 1 explains homogeneous solutions, their classification into nine physical state combinations, and methods for expressing concentration including mass percentage, volume percentage, mass by volume percentage, parts per million, mole fraction, molarity, and molality. It covers the solubility of solids and gases in liquids, Henry's law and its practical applications, vapour pressure of liquid solutions, and Raoult's law for volatile and non-volatile solutes. The chapter distinguishes ideal and non-ideal solutions showing positive or negative deviations, defines minimum- and maximum-boiling azeotropes, and derives the four colligative properties—relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure—for molar mass determination, along with the van ’t Hoff factor for abnormal molar masses due to association or dissociation.

qa.q: What is a solution and what are its two main components?
qa.a: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more chemically non-reacting substances whose composition can vary within certain limits. Its two components are the solvent (present in a larger amount, determining the physical state) and the solute (present in a smaller amount, dissolving in the solvent).

qa.q: How do molarity and molality differ with respect to temperature?
qa.a: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution and changes with temperature because solution volume changes with temperature. Molality is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent and is independent of temperature because mass does not change with temperature.

qa.q: Why does mole fraction have no unit?
qa.a: Mole fraction is the ratio of the number of moles of one component to the total number of moles of all components in the solution, and since both numerator and denominator are expressed in moles, it is dimensionless.

qa.q: How does temperature affect the solubility of a solid in a liquid?
qa.a: If the dissolution process is endothermic (absorbs heat), solubility generally increases with an increase in temperature. If the dissolution process is exothermic (releases heat), solubility generally decreases with an increase in temperature.
qa.section: 1.3.1 Solubility of a Solid in a Liquid

qa.q: State Henry's law and write its mathematical expression.
qa.a: Henry's law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid: \(p = K_H x\), where \(p\) is partial pressure, \(x\) is mole fraction of the dissolved gas, and \(K_H\) is Henry's law constant.
qa.section: 1.3.2 Solubility of a Gas in a Liquid (Henry's Law)

qa.q: What are the main applications of Henry's law?
qa.a: Henry's law explains the sealing of carbonated drinks under high pressure to dissolve CO2, decompression sickness in scuba divers ascending too quickly due to nitrogen bubbles in the blood, and lower blood oxygen levels at high altitudes where partial pressure of oxygen is lower.
qa.section: 1.3.2 Solubility of a Gas in a Liquid (Henry's Law)

qa.q: State Raoult's law for a solution of volatile liquids.
qa.a: Raoult's law states that the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component of a solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution at a given temperature: \(p_A = x_A p_A^\circ\) and \(p_B = x_B p_B^\circ\).
qa.section: 1.4.1 Vapour Pressure of Liquid–Liquid Solutions (Raoult's Law)

qa.q: Under what condition is Raoult's law a special case of Henry's law?
qa.a: Raoult's law becomes a special case of Henry's law when the Henry's law constant \(K_H\) is equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component \(p_A^\circ\).
qa.section: 1.4.2 Raoult’s Law as a Special Case of Henry’s Law

qa.q: What are the characteristics of an ideal solution?
qa.a: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law at all compositions, has A–B intermolecular attractions nearly equal to A–A and B–B attractions, has zero enthalpy change on mixing (\(\Delta H_{\text{mix}} = 0\)), and has zero volume change on mixing (\(\Delta V_{\text{mix}} = 0\)).

qa.q: What are azeotropes and what are their two types?
qa.a: Azeotropes are liquid mixtures that boil at a constant temperature and have the same composition in the liquid and vapour phases, so they cannot be separated by simple fractional distillation. They are classified into minimum-boiling azeotropes (large positive deviation, e.g., ethanol and water) and maximum-boiling azeotropes (large negative deviation, e.g., nitric acid and water).

qa.q: What are colligative properties? List the four main colligative properties.
qa.a: Colligative properties are properties of dilute solutions that depend on the number of solute particles relative to solvent particles rather than on the chemical nature of the solute. The four main colligative properties are relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure.
qa.section: 1.6 Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass

qa.q: Why is osmotic pressure preferred for determining the molar mass of proteins and polymers?
qa.a: Osmotic pressure is measured at room temperature, which prevents thermal decomposition of heat-sensitive biomolecules like proteins, and uses molarity rather than molality.

qa.q: What is the van ’t Hoff factor and how does its value indicate association or dissociation?
qa.a: The van ’t Hoff factor \(i\) is the ratio of the observed colligative property to the calculated colligative property (or normal molar mass to observed molar mass). For non-electrolytes \(i = 1\), for solute association \(i < 1\), and for solute dissociation \(i > 1\).
